before.text: Does the agent provide meaningful explainability per EU AI Act Article 13 and IEEE 7001:2021 transparency process requirements for all intelligence outputs?
before.l1: No explainability; AI intelligence outputs are black-box with no explanation of reasoning, confidence, or input data usage
before.l3: Agent provides post-hoc explanations for key outputs using LIME/SHAP-style attribution, but does not implement IEEE 7001 transparency process documentation
before.l5: Full IEEE 7001 transparency with human-interpretable explanations per EU AI Act Art. 13, causal chain documentation, uncertainty quantification, and explainability accessibility for non-technical stakeholders

after.text: Does the agent attach an explanation to every intelligence output and supply instructions for use covering capabilities, limitations and output interpretation, as EU AI Act Art. 13 requires for high-risk systems (Annex III systems from 2 December 2027)?
after.l1: Outputs ship with no stated inputs, confidence or limitations, and no instructions for use exist.
after.l3: Explanations (e.g. feature attribution) are attached to some output types, or instructions for use omit at least one Art. 13(3)(b) item (capabilities, limitations, output interpretation).
after.l5: Every output type carries an explanation record (main inputs, confidence or uncertainty, known limitations); instructions for use cover each Art. 13(3)(b) item; an automated test per release fails when an output type ships without its explanation record.

before.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 50(1) GPAI transparency by (1) clearly disclosing when outputs are AI-generated/AI-assisted, (2) providing provenance (model/system identity, version, and data sources categories), and (3) ensuring disclosures persist across downstream exports/APIs and are auditable (logs/evidence bundles)?
before.l1: No GPAI transparency: outputs are presented as human-authored or source-verified with no disclosure or provenance
before.l3: Discloses AI use in some UI surfaces, but provenance and persistence across exports/APIs are inconsistent and not auditable
before.l5: Full Art. 50(1) transparency with consistent disclosure, machine-readable provenance metadata, downstream persistence, and audit-ready disclosure logs for every intelligence artifact

after.text: Does the agent inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system, at the latest at the first interaction, unless this is obvious from the context (EU AI Act Art. 50(1), applicable from 2 August 2026)?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(1); EU AI Act Art. 50(5)
after.l1: No AI-interaction disclosure on any channel.
after.l3: Disclosure at first interaction on the primary channel, but missing or untested on at least one other channel in use (e.g. voice, email, API-delivered replies).
after.l5: Disclosure at first interaction on every channel in the channel inventory, in an accessible format, with an automated regression test per channel and a recorded rationale for each 'obvious from context' exception.

citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 50(1); EU AI Act Art. 50(5)

before.text: For decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, does the agent implement GDPR Article 22(3) safeguards by enabling (1) human intervention, (2) user ability to express their point of view, and (3) contestation/appeal with documented outcomes, timelines, and audit trails?
before.l1: No safeguard workflow; users cannot request human review or contest outcomes, and decisions are final/opaque
before.l3: Offers a manual escalation path, but viewpoint capture, decision logging, and appeal outcomes are inconsistently recorded
before.l5: End-to-end Art. 22(3) rights workflow with SLA-tracked human review, user submissions, reasoned decisions, outcome notifications, and immutable audit logs linking model outputs to human determinations

after.text: For decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, does the agent implement GDPR Article 22(3) safeguards by enabling (1) human intervention, (2) user ability to express their point of view, and (3) contestation/appeal with documented outcomes, timelines, and audit trails?
after.l1: No human-intervention, point-of-view or contestation route for decisions within Art. 22.
after.l3: A manual escalation route exists, but requests, submitted viewpoints and outcomes are not recorded per decision.
after.l5: Each Art. 22 decision exposes all three safeguards; every request is logged with timestamps, the human reviewer, the outcome and reasons; response times are measured against a documented target.

before.text: Does the agent operationalize NIST AI RMF GOVERN by defining accountable roles (RACI), escalation triggers (harm, drift, bias), incident response playbooks, and third-party/model-provider governance (due diligence, monitoring, and termination criteria) for intelligence systems?
before.l1: No operational governance; no defined roles, triggers, or incident playbooks for AI issues
before.l3: Defines some roles and incident handling, but escalation triggers, third-party governance, and evidence are incomplete
before.l5: Full GOVERN implementation with accountable roles, measurable triggers, incident playbooks, third-party governance, and audit-ready governance evidence

after.text: Does the agent operationalize NIST AI RMF GOVERN by keeping a register of the legal and regulatory requirements that apply to it (GOVERN 1.1) and defining accountable roles (RACI), escalation triggers (harm, drift, bias), incident response playbooks, and third-party/model-provider governance (due diligence, monitoring, and termination criteria)?
after.l1: No documented AI roles, escalation triggers, incident playbook or legal-requirements register.
after.l3: Roles and an incident playbook are documented, but escalation triggers lack thresholds, the legal-requirements register is missing or stale, or model providers lack due-diligence and termination criteria.
after.l5: Legal-requirements register reviewed at least annually; RACI covering each GOVERN category; escalation triggers with measurable thresholds; playbook exercised at least once with records; due diligence, monitoring and termination criteria on file for every model provider.

before.text: Where the agent integrates a general-purpose AI model, does the program obtain and keep current the information and documentation the model provider must supply to downstream providers under EU AI Act Article 53(1)(b), and use it in the agent's own risk assessment?
before.l1: The model's capabilities and limitations are not documented by the integrator
before.l3: Provider documentation is collected once, but it is not tracked across model versions or used in risk assessment
before.l5: Provider documentation versioned per model release, limitations mapped to agent risks and controls, and model upgrades gated on reviewing the new documentation

after.text: Where the agent generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, are outputs marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated, with systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 compliant by 2 December 2026 (EU AI Act Art. 50(2); Art. 111(4) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(2); EU AI Act Art. 111(4) (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
after.l1: Generated outputs carry no machine-readable marking.
after.l3: Marking applied to some generated modalities; detection not verified by test for at least one generated modality.
after.l5: Every generated modality is marked; detection is verified by test per modality; marking survives the agent's export and API paths; conformance is mapped to the Commission Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content (10 June 2026).

citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 50(2); EU AI Act Art. 111(4) (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)

after.text: When the agent integrates a third-party general-purpose AI model, does its provider obtain and retain the model provider's information and documentation for integrators (EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(b), Annex XII), pin the model version, and record whether its own modifications are significant enough to make it a GPAI model provider?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(b); EU AI Act Annex XII
after.l1: Model used without the provider's integrator documentation or a pinned version.
after.l3: Integrator documentation stored and model version pinned, but no recorded assessment of whether the agent's fine-tuning or modification is significant.
after.l5: Documentation retained per pinned model version; a capability and limitation register linked to agent tasks; a written modification-significance assessment against the Commission GPAI guidelines; re-review triggered by every model version change.

citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(b); EU AI Act Annex XII

after.text: Where the agent is used to make significant decisions about California consumers, does the business give a Pre-use Notice (§7220) and handle requests to opt out of automated decisionmaking technology as §7221 requires, with compliance in place by 1 January 2027 for uses that began earlier (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11 §7200(b))?
after.regulatoryRef: CPPA ADMT regulations, Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11 §7200(b); CPPA ADMT regulations §7220; CPPA ADMT regulations §7221
after.l1: No inventory of ADMT used for significant decisions and no Pre-use Notice.
after.l3: Pre-use Notice published; opt-out requests handled manually without a tracked response record.
after.l5: ADMT inventory covers every significant-decision use; Pre-use Notice delivered before use; every opt-out request logged with response timestamps; evidence in place before 1 January 2027.

citations.after: CPPA ADMT regulations, Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11 §7200(b); CPPA ADMT regulations §7220; CPPA ADMT regulations §7221

after.text: For a high-risk AI system it provides, is the agent designed so that the people overseeing it can disregard, override or reverse its output and interrupt it through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure (EU AI Act Art. 14(4)(d)-(e), applicable to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027)?
after.l1: No override or interrupt control available to the people overseeing the agent.
after.l3: Individual outputs can be overridden, but there is no tested interrupt ('stop') procedure, or it does not cover every deployment channel.
after.l5: Every deployment gives named overseers an override-and-reverse control and a stop procedure; the stop procedure is tested on each release with the time to halt recorded; every override and stop is logged with the overseer's identity.

before.text: Does the agent prevent discriminatory automated decisions per GDPR Article 22 and EU AI Act Article 10 data governance for training data bias?
before.regulatoryRef: GDPR Art. 22; EU AI Act Art. 10(3)
before.l1: No discrimination prevention; automated profiling and decisions may discriminate based on protected characteristics without detection or mitigation
before.l3: Agent performs periodic bias audits and applies post-processing bias mitigation, but does not implement continuous discrimination monitoring or pre-processing data governance
before.l5: Full non-discrimination governance with continuous bias monitoring across protected characteristics, pre-processing data representativeness assessment per EU AI Act Art. 10(3), GDPR Art. 22 human review for significant decisions, and bias incident reporting

after.text: For a high-risk AI system it provides, does the agent's provider examine training, validation and testing data for possible biases and apply measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them (EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), applicable to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027), limiting any processing of special categories of personal data for that purpose to what is strictly necessary (Art. 4a)?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)-(g); EU AI Act Art. 4a (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
after.l1: No documented bias examination of training, validation or testing data; special-category personal data used for bias work without a recorded necessity decision.
after.l3: Documented bias examination with named metrics exists for some but not all of the training, validation and testing data sets, or special-category processing lacks a written strict-necessity record.
after.l5: Bias examination records with metrics and mitigation actions exist for training, validation and testing data for every release; each special-category processing for bias correction has a strict-necessity record, an access log and a deletion record; examination re-runs on each dataset change.

citations.before: GDPR Art. 22; EU AI Act Art. 10(3)
citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)-(g); EU AI Act Art. 4a (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)

before.text: Does the agent implement AI system lifecycle management per ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A controls including risk assessment and continuous improvement?
before.l1: No AI management system; intelligence AI operates without systematic risk assessment, monitoring, or improvement processes
before.l3: Agent maintains basic AI system documentation and performs periodic risk assessments, but does not implement full ISO 42001 Annex A control set
before.l5: Full ISO 42001 AIMS implementation with Annex A controls, continuous AI risk assessment and treatment, AI system performance monitoring, stakeholder impact assessment, and systematic improvement cycle documentation

after.text: Does the agent implement AI system lifecycle management per ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A controls including risk assessment and continuous improvement?
after.l1: No AI management system: no AI policy, AI risk assessment record or statement of applicability.
after.l3: AI policy and an AI risk assessment exist, but there is no statement of applicability for the Annex A controls, or no internal audit or management review on record.
after.l5: AIMS scope, AI policy, AI risk assessment and treatment records, statement of applicability for Annex A controls, and an internal audit and management review within the last 12 months; nonconformities tracked to closure.

before.text: Does the agent implement NIST AI RMF Map function requirements for contextual risk identification in deployed intelligence systems?
before.l1: No AI risk mapping; deployed intelligence systems lack systematic contextualization of risks and impacts
before.l3: Agent performs initial risk mapping per NIST AI RMF MAP function, but does not maintain continuous risk categorization or impact assessment updates
before.l5: Full NIST AI RMF MAP function implementation with continuous risk categorization, impact assessment across stakeholder categories, risk tolerance documentation, and integration with MEASURE and MANAGE functions

after.text: Does the agent implement NIST AI RMF Map function requirements for contextual risk identification in deployed intelligence systems?
after.l1: No record of intended purpose, deployment context or applicable laws for deployed intelligence systems.
after.l3: MAP records (intended purpose, context and applicable laws per MAP 1.1, risk categorisation) exist for some deployed systems, or were not updated after the last material change.
after.l5: Every deployed system has MAP records covering MAP 1.1-5.2, including impact characterisation; records are updated on each material change and linked to MEASURE and MANAGE entries.

before.text: Does the agent enforce data minimization per GDPR Article 5(1)(c) in intelligence generation, preventing unnecessary personal data retention in AI inference pipelines?
before.l1: No data minimization in AI pipelines; personal data is retained indefinitely in training data, model weights, and inference caches without purpose review
before.l3: Agent implements retention policies and periodically reviews data necessity, but does not enforce automated data minimization in AI inference or implement right to erasure in model artifacts
before.l5: Full data minimization with automated retention enforcement per GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), differential privacy in training pipelines, right to erasure implementation covering model artifacts, inference cache purging, and privacy-preserving intelligence generation

after.text: Does the agent enforce data minimization per GDPR Article 5(1)(c) in intelligence generation, preventing unnecessary personal data retention in AI inference pipelines?
after.l1: No retention limits or purpose review for personal data in prompts, logs, training data or inference caches.
after.l3: Documented purpose and retention periods for some stores (e.g. logs) but not for inference caches or training datasets, or erasure requests are not propagated to them.
after.l5: Every store holding personal data (prompts, logs, caches, training and fine-tuning sets) has a documented purpose and a retention period enforced by automated deletion; erasure requests reach every store with completion records.

before.text: Does the agent align with UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation 2021 Principle 4 (Data Protection) and Principle 9 (Privacy and Oversight) in intelligence personalization?
before.l1: No ethics alignment; intelligence personalization operates without UNESCO ethics principle integration or human oversight mechanisms
before.l3: Agent implements basic human oversight checkpoints and respects user privacy preferences, but does not systematically assess UNESCO ethics principle alignment
before.l5: Full UNESCO ethics alignment with Principles 4/9 integration, human oversight architecture per Principle 9, ethical impact assessment for intelligence systems, stakeholder engagement in ethics governance, and public transparency reporting

after.text: Does the agent's personalization keep humans able to review and override its decisions, as set out in the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI principle 'Human oversight and determination'?

after.l1: No human review or override path for personalization decisions.
after.l3: A human review path exists for some personalization decision types, but overrides are not logged or are not available to affected users.
after.l5: Every personalization decision type has a named human reviewer with an override control; overrides and outcomes are logged and reviewed on a documented schedule.

citations.after: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021): Human oversight and determination

before.text: Does the agent support human agency per OECD AI Principles 1.3 (Transparency and Explainability) and 1.4 (Robustness) in intelligence systems affecting material decisions?
before.l1: No human agency support; intelligence systems make recommendations without transparency or robustness validation
before.l3: Agent supports human review of AI recommendations and provides explanations, but does not implement OECD robustness requirements or contestability mechanisms
before.l5: Full OECD principle compliance with human agency preservation, contestability mechanisms for material AI decisions, robustness testing per Principle 1.4, transparency documentation per Principle 1.3, and regular accountability assessments

after.text: Does the agent support human agency in intelligence systems affecting material decisions, per OECD AI Principles 1.3 'Transparency and explainability' and 1.4 'Robustness, security and safety' (OECD/LEGAL/0449, amended 3 May 2024)?
after.regulatoryRef: OECD AI Principles 1.3 Transparency and explainability; OECD AI Principles 1.4 Robustness, security and safety
after.l1: Material-decision recommendations carry no explanation, no robustness test record, and no route for affected people to contest them.
after.l3: Explanations and a human review route exist, but there is no documented robustness testing or no contestation channel for affected people.
after.l5: Human agency preserved with contestability mechanisms for material AI decisions, documented robustness testing, transparency documentation for each decision type, and a recorded accountability review on a fixed schedule.

citations.after: OECD AI Principles 1.3 Transparency and explainability; OECD AI Principles 1.4 Robustness, security and safety

before.text: Does the agent implement adversarial robustness per NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6 and OWASP ML Security Top 10 for model extraction and inference attacks?

before.l1: No adversarial robustness; intelligence models are vulnerable to extraction, evasion, and poisoning attacks without detection
before.l3: Agent implements basic input validation and anomaly detection, but does not perform systematic adversarial testing or implement OWASP ML security controls
before.l5: Full adversarial robustness with NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6 metrics, adversarial testing per OWASP ML Top 10, model extraction prevention, inference attack detection, continuous robustness monitoring, and incident response for AI security events

after.text: Does the agent evaluate and document its security and resilience per NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.7, with adversarial tests covering at least prompt injection, model extraction, excessive agency and tool misuse?

after.l3: Adversarial tests run before release for some of the named categories; results documented but not re-run on model, prompt or tool changes.
after.l5: A documented test suite covers each named category and every further category in the agent's threat model, runs on each model, prompt or tool change, blocks release on failure, and stores results as MEASURE 2.7 evidence.

citations.before: NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6; OWASP ML Top 10

before.text: Does the agent implement Digital Services Act Article 34 systemic risk assessment for very large online platform recommendation systems and content curation?

after.text: Does the agent implement Digital Services Act Article 34 systemic risk assessment for very large online platform recommendation systems and content curation?

before.text: Does the agent issue a DSA Article 17(1) statement of reasons for each content moderation decision (removal, restriction, demonetization, suspension), including (a) decision type and legal/ToS basis, (b) main parameters/facts relied on, (c) whether automated tools were used, and (d) clear redress/complaint options?

after.text: Does the agent issue a DSA Article 17(1) statement of reasons for each content moderation decision (removal, restriction, demonetization, suspension), including (a) decision type and legal/ToS basis, (b) main parameters/facts relied on, (c) whether automated tools were used, and (d) clear redress/complaint options?

after.l3: Statements are issued for some restriction types, or omit an Art. 17(3) element (facts, use of automated means, legal or contractual ground, redress).

before.text: Does the agent prevent self-preferencing in ranking/recommendation and related access conditions per DMA Article 5(2), ensuring that the platform does not treat its own content/services more favorably than third-party content/services (including through ranking, recommendation, default placements, or preferential interface access)?

before.l3: Implements a fairness policy and some monitoring, but parity testing is incomplete and exceptions/defaults are not consistently governed
before.l5: Full Art. 5(2) compliance with parity-by-design ranking controls, continuous self-preference detection (A/B audits), default-placement governance, third-party parity KPIs, and audit-ready evidence for regulator review

after.text: Where the platform is a designated gatekeeper, does the agent avoid treating the gatekeeper's own services and products more favourably in ranking and related indexing and crawling than similar third-party services, applying transparent, fair and non-discriminatory ranking conditions (EU DMA Art. 6(5))?
after.l1: No parity controls: the gatekeeper's own services can be ranked more favourably with no detection or record.
after.l3: Ranking conditions are documented, but parity tests do not cover every ranking change or deviations are not recorded.
after.l5: Ranking conditions documented and available to business users; parity tests comparing own and third-party services run on every ranking change; deviations recorded with reasons; test records retained.

before.text: Does the agent implement EU Copyright Directive 2019/790 Article 17 OCSSP obligations end-to-end: (a) best-efforts licensing/authorization, (b) best-efforts to ensure unavailability of notified works, (c) stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, (d) safeguards for lawful uses (quotation/criticism/review, parody/pastiche), and (e) effective complaint and redress with timely human review?

before.l3: Implements some detection/licensing workflows, but lawful-use safeguards and complaint/redress timeliness are inconsistent
before.l5: Full Art. 17 compliance with licensing workflows, stay-down controls tied to substantiated notices, exception-preserving safeguards, timely human review, and audit-ready evidence of proportionality and redress outcomes

after.text: Does the agent implement EU Copyright Directive 2019/790 Article 17 OCSSP obligations end-to-end: (a) best-efforts licensing/authorization, (b) best-efforts to ensure unavailability of notified works, (c) stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, (d) safeguards for lawful uses (quotation/criticism/review, parody/pastiche), and (e) effective complaint and redress with timely human review?

before.l3: Provides an online privacy notice and some parent notices, but disclosures are incomplete or not delivered at the required time/before collection
before.l5: Full §312.3 compliance with complete online privacy notice, timely direct parental notice prior to collection, versioned notice retention, and evidence logs supporting enforcement/audit readiness

before.text: Does the agent implement EU Media Freedom Act 2024 Article 4-aligned safeguards for media integrity, including protection of editorial independence/non-interference and user/recipient-facing transparency about editorial/recommender influence over news/media prominence?

after.text: On a very large online platform, does the agent provide the functionality for media service providers to declare their status (Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 Art. 18(1)) and apply the Art. 18 procedural safeguards before restricting or suspending their content?

after.l3: Ownership and licence scope are documented, but contribution and provenance evidence is missing for some inventions.
after.l5: Every partnership invention has inventorship and ownership records, a licence scope (field of use, sublicensing) covering the Art. 28(1) acts, and retained contribution and provenance logs.

before.text: Does the agent comply with WIPO WPPT Article 7 (performers right of reproduction) by ensuring that partnership projects involving recorded performances (including AI voice/performance capture and synthetic performance generation) have (1) performer consent and scope-limited reproduction licenses, (2) fixation and reproduction tracking, (3) attribution/royalty allocation terms where applicable, and (4) evidence logs linking each use to the relevant authorization?
before.l1: No WPPT controls: performances are ingested/reproduced/republished via AI tools without performer-authorized reproduction rights or evidence of consent
before.l3: Obtains consent in common cases, but scope limitations (media/territory/term), AI-specific reproduction tracking, and evidence retention are inconsistent
before.l5: Full WPPT Art. 7 compliance with structured performer consent + reproduction licensing, AI capture/synthesis usage logging, scope enforcement (term/territory/media), attribution/royalty metadata, and audit-ready proof of authorization for every reproduction

after.text: Where partnership projects reproduce performances fixed in phonograms, including through AI voice capture or training, does the agent hold the performers' authorisation for each reproduction (WIPO WPPT Art. 7) and keep evidence linking each use to that authorisation?
after.l1: Fixed performances are reproduced through AI tools with no record of performer authorisation.
after.l3: Authorisation obtained in common cases, but scope (media, territory, term) is not recorded or not checked before reproduction.
after.l5: Every reproduction of a fixed performance is linked to a recorded authorisation with scope; scope checked before each use; evidence retained.

before.text: Does the agent protect trade secrets in partnership data access/sharing under the EU Data Act Article 24 by (1) classifying trade-secret elements in shared datasets, (2) applying technical/organizational safeguards (access controls, secure enclaves/redaction, purpose limitation), (3) enforcing confidentiality + non-disclosure terms downstream, and (4) maintaining evidence to justify withholding/restricting trade-secret data where permitted?
before.l1: No Art. 24 safeguards: partnership data sharing exposes trade secrets without classification, redaction, or enforceable confidentiality controls
before.l3: Implements basic confidentiality and access controls, but trade-secret classification/redaction and downstream enforcement/audit evidence are incomplete
before.l5: Full Data Act Art. 24 trade secret governance with granular classification, redaction/enclave sharing patterns, contract + technical enforcement of confidentiality, and audit-ready evidence supporting any restrictions/withholding decisions

after.text: When partnership data access or sharing under the EU Data Act includes trade secrets, does the agent disclose them only after the trade secrets are identified and the protective measures to preserve their confidentiality are agreed with the user (Art. 4(6)) or the third party (Art. 5(9))?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 4(6); EU Data Act Art. 5(9)
after.l1: Trade secrets in shared data are disclosed without identification or agreed protective measures.
after.l3: Trade secrets are identified for some datasets, or disclosure proceeds before the agreed measures are in place for at least one recipient.
after.l5: Every shared dataset has its trade-secret elements identified, including in metadata; disclosure is gated on a recorded agreement of protective measures per recipient; every gate decision is logged.

citations.after: EU Data Act Art. 4(6); EU Data Act Art. 5(9)

after.text: Does the agent produce, for each build of software it generates or assembles, a software bill of materials in a commonly used, machine-readable format covering at least the top-level dependencies, as the Cyber Resilience Act requires from 11 December 2027 (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Annex I Part II(1))?
